questions.explain: IR 8286C describes cyber risks being recorded in CSRRs at lower levels, aggregated upward, normalized into the enterprise risk register, and summarized in the enterprise risk profile that leadership oversees.

questions.stem: Which CSF 2.0 Subcategory states that cybersecurity risk management activities are included in enterprise risk management processes?
options: GV.RM-03
GV.OC-02
ID.RA-05
GV.OV-01
questions.explain: GV.RM-03 brings cyber risk management activities into ERM. GV.OC-02 covers stakeholder expectations, ID.RA-05 uses threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact to understand inherent risk, and GV.OV-01 reviews strategy outcomes.

questions.case: A bank's board receives separate reports for credit, liquidity and operational risk, but cyber risk arrives as a technical vulnerability list that directors cannot compare with other risks. The CRO wants cyber risk reported in the same terms as other enterprise risks.
questions.stem: Which NIST resource is most directly designed to help with this?
options: NIST SP 800-61 incident handling guidance
The NIST IR 8286 series on integrating cybersecurity and ERM
The NIST Privacy Framework
NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 on C-SCRM
questions.explain: The IR 8286 series explains how to express cyber risk in risk registers and roll it into the enterprise risk register and profile, so it can be compared with other risks. SP 800-61 covers incident response, the Privacy Framework covers privacy risk, and SP 800-161 covers supply chain.

questions.stem: In CSF 2.0, where does cybersecurity supply chain risk management sit?
options: IDENTIFY, as ID.SC
PROTECT, as PR.SC
GOVERN, as GV.SC
It was removed and moved to SP 800-161
questions.explain: CSF 2.0 moved supply chain risk management from IDENTIFY (ID.SC in 1.1) to GOVERN as GV.SC, with 10 Subcategories. There is no PR.SC Category. SP 800-161 adds detailed guidance but does not replace GV.SC.

questions.case: A software firm's C-SCRM work is a vendor questionnaire run by procurement. There is no strategy, no named owners, no budget, and supplier risks never reach the enterprise risk register. A recent breach at a code-signing vendor went unnoticed for weeks.
questions.stem: Which pair of GV.SC outcomes addresses the most fundamental gaps?
options: GV.SC-05 contract requirements and GV.SC-10 post-termination activities
GV.SC-04 supplier criticality and GV.SC-09 lifecycle integration
GV.SC-06 due diligence and GV.SC-08 incident planning with suppliers
GV.SC-01 program, strategy and policies, and GV.SC-03 integration into cyber and enterprise risk management
questions.explain: The core gaps are that no C-SCRM program, strategy or ownership exists (GV.SC-01) and that supplier risk is not integrated with cyber and enterprise risk management (GV.SC-03). The other pairs are real outcomes, but they build on a program the firm does not yet have.

questions.stem: A company certified to ISO/IEC 27001 must show a US customer how its controls support CSF 2.0 outcomes. What should it use?
options: Informative References mapping CSF outcomes to ISO/IEC 27001
A CSF 2.0 certificate from an accredited body
CSF Implementation Tiers
The CSF 1.1 Framework Core document
questions.explain: Informative References map CSF outcomes to standards such as ISO/IEC 27001, so existing controls can serve as evidence. No CSF certification exists, Tiers describe rigor rather than control mappings, and CSF 1.1 is superseded.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about using the CSF with other NIST and ISO frameworks are correct? Select TWO.
options: NIST states the Privacy Framework and the CSF can be used together to manage cybersecurity and privacy risks
A mapping to SP 800-53 means implementing the CSF automatically satisfies every SP 800-53 control
SP 800-53 is used as an Informative Reference showing controls that help achieve CSF outcomes
ISO/IEC 27001 replaces the CSF Core for organizations outside the US
Informative References are fixed and can only change when a new CSF version is released
questions.explain: NIST says the Privacy Framework and CSF can be used together, and SP 800-53 is a key Informative Reference. A mapping shows relationships, not full equivalence. ISO/IEC 27001 does not replace the Core, and References are online and updated more often than the CSF.

questions.stem: For each statement about CSF Informative References, select Yes if true.

statements.s: They map CSF Core outcomes to existing standards, guidelines and regulations.
They can be accessed and exported through the CSF 2.0 Reference Tool.
They are printed in full inside the CSF 2.0 document and never change.

questions.explain: Informative References map Core outcomes to other content and are available online through the CSF 2.0 Reference Tool in human- and machine-readable formats. They are kept outside the CSF document so they can be updated more often.

questions.stem: Under the EU AI Act, which risk tier covers AI practices that are banned outright and cannot be made lawful through compliance measures?
options: High risk
Limited (transparency) risk
Unacceptable risk
Systemic risk
questions.explain: Unacceptable-risk practices are listed in Art. 5 and prohibited. High-risk systems are allowed if they meet strict requirements. Limited risk carries only transparency duties. Systemic risk is a category of GPAI model, not a tier of banned practices.

questions.stem: A police force wants an AI tool that flags individuals as likely future offenders based only on personality traits and demographic profiling. How does the AI Act treat this?
options: Prohibited under Article 5
High-risk under Annex III law enforcement
Permitted with a fundamental rights impact assessment
Limited risk requiring a disclosure notice
questions.explain: Assessing a person's risk of offending based solely on profiling or personality traits is a prohibited practice. Law-enforcement AI that supports a human assessment based on objective, verifiable facts is high-risk instead. A FRIA or disclosure cannot make a banned practice lawful.

questions.stem: For each statement about Article 5 prohibited practices, select Yes if true.

statements.s: The social scoring ban applies to private companies as well as public authorities.
A manipulative technique is prohibited only if it is subliminal.
Exploiting vulnerabilities due to a person's specific social or economic situation can be a prohibited practice.

questions.explain: The final text bans social scoring by public and private actors. The manipulation ban covers subliminal, purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques that cause significant harm, not only subliminal ones. Exploiting vulnerabilities linked to age, disability or social or economic situation is banned.

questions.stem: A university plans to use webcam AI during lectures to detect students' boredom and frustration so lecturers can adjust teaching. Which classification applies?
options: High-risk under Annex III education
Limited risk; students must be informed under Article 50(3)
Minimal risk, as no decision is made about students
Prohibited, because it is emotion recognition in education
questions.explain: Inferring emotions in education institutions is banned unless it is for medical or safety reasons. Outside work and education, emotion recognition is high-risk with an Art. 50(3) notice duty, but neither applies here. Whether a decision is made does not matter.

questions.stem: Which activity is a prohibited AI practice under Article 5?
options: Using facial verification to unlock a smartphone
Untargeted scraping of CCTV footage to expand a facial recognition database
Retrospective biometric identification under judicial authorisation
Detecting pilot fatigue from eye movements for safety reasons
questions.explain: Untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV to build or expand facial recognition databases is banned. 1:1 verification is excluded from the biometric rules. Post (retrospective) RBI is high-risk, not banned. Emotion or fatigue detection for safety reasons is carved out of the workplace ban.

questions.case: A Member State's law allows police to use real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces. Officers propose several uses at a large public event.
questions.stem: Which uses could fall within the Article 5 exceptions, assuming prior authorisation and other safeguards are met? Select TWO.
options: A targeted search for a specific abducted child
Scanning all attendees to find people with unpaid parking fines
Locating a named suspect of a listed serious crime punishable by at least four years
Building a watch-list of protest organisers for later reference
Measuring crowd sentiment toward the government
questions.explain: The exceptions cover targeted searches for victims of abduction, trafficking or sexual exploitation and for missing persons, preventing imminent threats to life or terrorism, and locating suspects of listed serious crimes. Minor offences, profiling protesters and sentiment analysis fall outside them.

questions.stem: A retailer uses AI on customers' faces to infer their likely religious beliefs for targeted advertising. What is the status of this system?
options: High-risk biometric categorisation under Annex III
Prohibited biometric categorisation inferring a sensitive characteristic
Limited risk; a notice under Article 50(3) is enough
Minimal risk because it is only used for marketing
questions.explain: Biometric categorisation that infers religious or philosophical beliefs, race, political opinions, trade-union membership, or sex life or orientation is prohibited. Annex III covers categorisation by other sensitive attributes, and an Art. 50(3) notice cannot cure a banned practice.

questions.stem: Which article classifies AI systems as high-risk because they are safety components of products covered by Annex I harmonisation legislation?
options: Article 5
Article 6(1)
Article 6(3)
Article 50
questions.explain: Art. 6(1) covers Annex I product-embedded AI that needs third-party conformity assessment. Art. 5 lists prohibitions. Art. 6(3) is the derogation for Annex III systems that pose no significant risk. Art. 50 sets transparency duties.

questions.case: MedScan sells an AI module that analyses X-ray images and is regulated as a medical device under the MDR. Under the MDR, the device needs assessment by a notified body.
questions.stem: How is the AI module classified under the AI Act, and how is conformity shown?
options: Minimal risk; MDR certification alone suffices
High-risk under Annex III; internal control self-assessment
High-risk under Art. 6(1); AI Act requirements are assessed within the MDR conformity procedure
Prohibited unless the Commission grants an exemption
questions.explain: A medical device needing third-party assessment under an Annex I law is high-risk under Art. 6(1), and the AI requirements are checked within the sectoral (MDR) procedure, typically by the same notified body. Medical devices are not an Annex III area, and nothing here is prohibited.

questions.stem: Which uses are listed as high-risk areas in Annex III? Select THREE.
options: Evaluating creditworthiness of natural persons
Filtering spam email
Screening job applications
Determining access to education institutions
Recommending products in an online shop
questions.explain: Credit scoring (essential services), CV screening (employment) and admission decisions (education) are Annex III areas. Spam filtering and product recommendations are typical minimal-risk uses.

questions.stem: A bank's AI is used only to detect fraudulent card transactions. How is it classified under Annex III point 5?
options: It is excluded: fraud detection is carved out of the credit-scoring entry
High-risk, because it relates to financial services
Prohibited, as it profiles customers
High-risk, requiring a FRIA by the bank
questions.explain: Annex III point 5 covers creditworthiness evaluation and credit scoring but expressly excludes systems used to detect financial fraud. Being financial alone does not make a system high-risk, and fraud detection is not a prohibited practice.

questions.case: An HR vendor's Annex III tool only reformats CVs into a standard template before human recruiters read them. The vendor wants to rely on Article 6(3).
questions.stem: For each statement, select Yes if true.

statements.s: The vendor may conclude the tool is not high-risk if it performs only a narrow procedural task and poses no significant risk.
If the vendor relies on Article 6(3), it no longer needs to document its assessment or register the system.
If the tool also profiled candidates, it would always be high-risk.

questions.explain: Art. 6(3) lets narrow procedural or preparatory systems escape high-risk status, but the provider must document the assessment and register the system. Annex III systems that profile natural persons are always high-risk.

questions.stem: Which high-risk requirement says training, validation and testing data must be relevant, sufficiently representative and examined for possible biases?
options: Article 9 Risk management system
Article 12 Record-keeping
Article 15 Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
Article 10 Data and data governance
questions.explain: Art. 10 sets data quality and bias-examination duties. Art. 9 is the lifecycle risk process. Art. 12 requires automatic logging. Art. 15 covers accuracy metrics, resilience and protection against attacks such as data poisoning.

questions.stem: A provider designs its high-risk system so an operator can interrupt it with a stop control and is warned against over-relying on its outputs. Which requirement does this mainly address?
options: Article 13 Transparency to deployers
Article 14 Human oversight
Article 11 Technical documentation
Article 17 Quality management system
questions.explain: Human oversight design includes the ability to override or stop the system and awareness of automation bias. Art. 13 is about instructions for use, Art. 11 about Annex IV documentation, and Art. 17 about the provider's QMS.

questions.stem: Article 15 requires resilience against AI-specific attacks. Which threats are named examples? Select THREE.
options: Data poisoning
Adversarial examples (model evasion)
Model poisoning
Phishing of the provider's sales staff
Physical theft of deployer laptops
questions.explain: Art. 15 names data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples or model evasion, confidentiality attacks and model flaws. Phishing and laptop theft are general security risks, not the AI-specific attacks the article lists.

questions.stem: A provider is bringing a new Annex III high-risk system to the EU market. Put the steps in order.
options: Complete the conformity assessment
Draw up the EU declaration of conformity and affix the CE marking
Place the system on the market
Run post-market monitoring and report serious incidents
questions.explain: Conformity is assessed first, then declared through the EU declaration of conformity and CE marking. Registration in the EU database also happens before placing on the market. Post-market monitoring follows release.

questions.stem: For most Annex III high-risk systems (points 2 to 8), which conformity assessment procedure applies?
options: Mandatory notified body assessment under Annex VII
Assessment by the AI Office
Internal control under Annex VI
No conformity assessment; registration only
questions.explain: Annex III points 2 to 8 use internal control (provider self-assessment, Annex VI). Notified bodies can be needed for biometric systems and Annex I products. The AI Office supervises GPAI models and does not certify high-risk systems. Registration does not replace assessment.

questions.case: Distributor Alpha buys a general HR analytics tool, rebrands it as 'AlphaHire', and markets it in the EU for ranking job candidates.
questions.stem: What is Alpha's status under the AI Act?
options: Deployer only
Distributor only, as it did not write the code
Importer, as long as it keeps the original documentation
Provider of a high-risk system, with full provider obligations
questions.explain: Under Art. 25, a distributor, importer or deployer that puts its name or trademark on a high-risk system, substantially modifies it, or changes its intended purpose so it becomes high-risk is treated as the provider. Writing the code is not required.

questions.stem: Which deployers must carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment before using an Annex III high-risk system? Select THREE.
options: A public body using AI to decide eligibility for social benefits
A private hospital operator providing public services
A car maker using AI to screen job applicants
An insurer using AI to price life insurance
A water utility using an AI safety component for its network
questions.explain: Art. 27 covers public-law bodies, private entities providing public services, and deployers of credit-scoring or life and health insurance pricing systems. A private car maker screening CVs is not in those groups, and critical-infrastructure systems (Annex III point 2) are excluded.

questions.stem: Under Article 26, for at least how long must deployers keep the logs automatically generated by a high-risk system under their control, unless other law says otherwise?
options: Six months
30 days
Ten years
Two years
questions.explain: Deployers keep automatically generated logs for at least six months. Ten years is the provider's document retention period. 30 days and two years are not AI Act figures for deployer logs.

questions.stem: For each statement about deployers of high-risk AI, select Yes if true.

statements.s: An employer must inform workers' representatives before using a high-risk system in the workplace.
A completed FRIA replaces the need for a GDPR data protection impact assessment.
After completing a FRIA, the deployer notifies the market surveillance authority of the results.

questions.explain: Employers must inform workers' representatives and affected workers. The FRIA complements a DPIA rather than replacing it. Art. 27 requires notifying the market surveillance authority of the FRIA results.

questions.stem: Who must make sure that synthetic images from a generative AI system are marked in a machine-readable format as artificially generated?
options: The deployer who publishes the image
The provider of the generative AI system
The national market surveillance authority
The notified body that assessed the system
questions.explain: Art. 50(2) puts machine-readable marking on the provider of the generative system. Deployers have the visible deepfake disclosure duty under Art. 50(4). Authorities and notified bodies do not mark content.

questions.case: A news site publishes an AI-written article on a public-interest election topic. A human editor reviews the article and the publisher takes editorial responsibility for it.
questions.stem: Does Article 50(4) require the site to disclose that the text was AI-generated?
options: Yes, AI-generated text must always be disclosed
Yes, but only through a machine-readable watermark
No, because only images and video are covered
No, because the text underwent human review and editorial responsibility
questions.explain: The public-interest text disclosure does not apply where the content has undergone human review or editorial control and someone holds editorial responsibility. Text is covered in general, and watermarking is a provider duty, not the deployer route here.

questions.stem: A company launches a customer-service chatbot on its website. Which Article 50 obligation applies to the chatbot's provider?
options: Register the chatbot in the EU database
Carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment
Design it so users are informed they are interacting with an AI system
Obtain CE marking before launch
questions.explain: Art. 50(1) requires providers to make sure people are told they are interacting with AI unless it is obvious. Registration, FRIA and CE marking are high-risk duties, and a general chatbot is not high-risk.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the AI Act's treatment of minimal-risk AI systems such as spam filters?
options: No new mandatory obligations as a risk class; voluntary codes of conduct are encouraged
They must be registered in the EU database
They need a simplified conformity assessment
They must carry a visible AI label
questions.explain: Minimal-risk systems get no new risk-specific obligations; Art. 95 encourages voluntary codes of conduct. General duties such as AI literacy and other laws like the GDPR still apply. Registration and conformity assessment are high-risk duties, and labels are Art. 50 duties.

questions.stem: A games studio voluntarily commits to applying bias testing and energy reporting to its non-high-risk AI features. Which AI Act mechanism is it using?
options: The GPAI Code of Practice under Article 56
A code of conduct under Article 95
An AI regulatory sandbox under Article 57
A harmonised standard under Article 40
questions.explain: Art. 95 codes of conduct let non-high-risk providers and deployers voluntarily apply requirements or wider goals. The Art. 56 Code of Practice is for GPAI model providers. Sandboxes are supervised testing environments. Harmonised standards give a presumption of conformity for high-risk requirements.

questions.stem: Which obligations apply to every general-purpose AI model provider under Article 53? Select THREE.
options: Publish a sufficiently detailed summary of training content
Adopt a policy to comply with EU copyright law
Provide information and documentation to downstream providers
Carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment
Obtain CE marking for the model
questions.explain: Art. 53 requires technical documentation, information for downstream providers, a copyright policy and a training-content summary. FRIA is a deployer duty for high-risk systems, and CE marking applies to high-risk systems, not GPAI models.

questions.stem: A provider releases a GPAI model with public weights under a free and open-source licence. The model does not have systemic risk. Which duty still applies?
options: None, open-source models are fully exempt
Only the Annex XI technical documentation
Only appointing an EU authorised representative
Publishing a training-content summary and putting a copyright policy in place
questions.explain: The open-source exemption removes the technical documentation duties to authorities and downstream providers. It does not remove the copyright policy or the training-content summary. The authorised-representative duty is also waived for qualifying open-source models without systemic risk.

questions.stem: Above what cumulative training compute is a GPAI model presumed to have high-impact capabilities, and so systemic risk?
options: 10^23 FLOPs
10^25 FLOPs
10^26 FLOPs
10^24 FLOPs
questions.explain: Art. 51 presumes high-impact capabilities above 10^25 floating-point operations of training compute. The Commission can update this threshold. 10^26 was the US reporting threshold under a now-revoked executive order and is a common distractor.

questions.stem: A lab's model is about to exceed the systemic-risk compute threshold. Put the steps in order.
options: The lab knows the training run will exceed 10^25 FLOPs
The lab notifies the Commission within two weeks
The model is treated as a GPAI model with systemic risk unless the lab's arguments are accepted
The lab performs model evaluations, adversarial testing and risk mitigation under Article 55
questions.explain: Art. 52 requires notification within two weeks of meeting the threshold or knowing it will be met. The provider may argue against classification. Once classified, the Art. 55 duties apply: evaluation, adversarial testing, mitigation, incident reporting and cybersecurity.

questions.stem: For each statement about GPAI models with systemic risk, select Yes if true.

statements.s: The Commission can designate a model as having systemic risk even if it was trained below 10^25 FLOPs.
Serious incidents involving the model are reported to a notified body.
Releasing the model under an open-source licence exempts it from Article 55 duties.

questions.explain: The Commission can designate models using Annex XIII criteria, whatever their compute. Serious incidents are reported to the AI Office (and national authorities where relevant), not notified bodies. The open-source exemption never applies to systemic-risk models.

questions.case: A provider of a mid-sized GPAI model without systemic risk wants to sign the GPAI Code of Practice to demonstrate compliance.
questions.stem: Which chapters of the Code are relevant to this provider?
options: Safety and Security only
All three, including Safety and Security
Transparency and Copyright
None; the Code applies only to systemic-risk models
questions.explain: The Transparency and Copyright chapters cover the Art. 53 duties of all GPAI providers. The Safety and Security chapter applies only to providers of models with systemic risk under Art. 55.

questions.stem: Which body has exclusive competence to supervise and enforce the obligations of general-purpose AI model providers?
options: The European Data Protection Board
National market surveillance authorities
The European Artificial Intelligence Board
The AI Office within the European Commission
questions.explain: The Commission, through the AI Office, supervises and enforces the GPAI model rules. Market surveillance authorities oversee most AI systems. The AI Board advises and coordinates but does not enforce. The EDPB handles GDPR consistency.

questions.stem: For each statement about the GPAI Code of Practice, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Signing the Code is mandatory for all GPAI providers placing models on the EU market.
A provider may sign only some chapters and show compliance with the others by other adequate means.
The Commission and the AI Board assessed the Code as an adequate voluntary tool for demonstrating compliance.

questions.explain: The Code is voluntary. Signatories can demonstrate compliance by adhering to it, and non-signatories use other adequate means. A provider can sign selected chapters; for example, one major provider signed only Safety and Security. The Commission and AI Board confirmed its adequacy in 2025.

questions.case: A software firm builds a recruitment screening system on top of a third-party GPAI model and needs to understand the model's limitations to meet its own high-risk obligations.
questions.stem: Which GPAI provider obligation most directly supports the firm?
options: Providing information and documentation to downstream providers
Publishing the training-content summary
Notifying the Commission of systemic risk
Adopting a copyright policy
questions.explain: Art. 53 requires GPAI providers to give downstream providers information and documentation (Annex XII) on capabilities and limitations so they can comply. The training summary is public-facing and high-level. Systemic-risk notification and copyright policy do not address the integrator's needs.

questions.stem: Which obligations apply only to providers of GPAI models with systemic risk, on top of the duties for all GPAI providers? Select TWO.
options: Perform model evaluation including adversarial testing
Publish a training-content summary
Ensure adequate cybersecurity for the model and its physical infrastructure
Draw up technical documentation for the AI Office
Adopt an EU copyright policy
questions.explain: Art. 55 adds model evaluation with adversarial testing, systemic risk assessment and mitigation, serious incident reporting, and cybersecurity. Training summaries, technical documentation and copyright policies are Art. 53 duties for every GPAI provider.

questions.stem: On what date did the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) enter into force?
options: 12 July 2024
2 February 2025
1 August 2024
2 August 2026
questions.explain: The Act was published in the Official Journal on 12 July 2024 and entered into force 20 days later, on 1 August 2024. 2 February 2025 is when the prohibitions began to apply, and 2 August 2026 is the general application date.

questions.stem: Why does the AI Act apply in all Member States without each one passing its own transposing law?
options: It is a directive with a direct-effect clause
It is a regulation, which is directly applicable
It is a Commission delegated act
The AI Office adopts it into each national legal system
questions.explain: EU regulations are binding and directly applicable in all Member States. Directives require national transposition. Delegated acts supplement existing legislation, and the AI Office has no power to adopt law into national systems. Member States still designate authorities and set penalty rules.

questions.stem: Which provisions began to apply on 2 February 2025? Select TWO.
options: Article 5 prohibited AI practices
Article 50 transparency obligations
Article 4 AI literacy
Annex III high-risk requirements
Article 53 GPAI provider obligations
questions.explain: Chapters I and II, including AI literacy (Art. 4) and the prohibitions (Art. 5), applied from 2 February 2025. GPAI duties applied from 2 August 2025, Art. 50 from 2 August 2026, and Annex III high-risk duties from 2 December 2027 after the omnibus.

questions.stem: A logistics firm uses only minimal-risk AI tools, such as route optimisation. Since 2 February 2025, which AI Act duty applies to it as a deployer?
options: Fundamental rights impact assessment
Registration in the EU database
Keeping logs for six months
Measures to promote AI literacy among staff operating the AI
questions.explain: Art. 4 AI literacy applies to providers and deployers of all AI systems, whatever their risk tier. FRIA, EU database registration and six-month log retention are tied to high-risk systems.

questions.stem: From which date did the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models begin to apply?
options: 2 August 2025
2 February 2025
2 August 2026
2 December 2027
questions.explain: Chapter V GPAI obligations, the governance bodies and the penalty rules applied from 2 August 2025. 2 February 2025 covers prohibitions and literacy. 2 August 2026 is general application. 2 December 2027 is the deferred Annex III date.

questions.case: ModelCo placed GPAI model A on the EU market in March 2025 and GPAI model B in October 2025.
questions.stem: For each statement, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Model B had to comply with Article 53 from its release.
Model A must comply with the GPAI obligations by 2 August 2027.
The Commission could fine ModelCo under Article 101 from 2 August 2025.

questions.explain: Models placed on the market from 2 August 2025 must comply immediately. Earlier models have until 2 August 2027. Although Chapter XII penalties applied from 2 August 2025, Art. 101 Commission fines on GPAI providers apply only from 2 August 2026.

questions.stem: Following the Digital Omnibus, which obligations still apply from 2 August 2026 for systems placed on the market from that date?
options: Annex III high-risk requirements
Article 50 transparency obligations
Annex I product-embedded high-risk requirements
The new non-consensual intimate imagery prohibition
questions.explain: Art. 50 transparency duties apply from 2 August 2026, the general application date. The omnibus moved Annex III to 2 December 2027 and Annex I to 2 August 2028. The new intimate-imagery and CSAM bans apply from 2 December 2026.

questions.case: GenPix launched an image-generation service in the EU in May 2026. A competitor launched a similar service in September 2026.
questions.stem: By when must each provider meet the Article 50(2) machine-readable marking duty?
options: Both by 2 August 2026
Both by 2 December 2026
GenPix by 2 August 2027; the competitor by 2 December 2026
GenPix by 2 December 2026; the competitor from its September 2026 launch
questions.explain: The omnibus gives generative systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 until 2 December 2026. Systems placed on the market after that date get no grace period and must comply from launch. 2 August 2027 is the legacy GPAI model deadline.

questions.stem: After the Digital Omnibus on AI, when do the obligations for Annex III stand-alone high-risk systems apply?
options: 2 August 2026
2 August 2028
2 December 2027
2 December 2026
questions.explain: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 deferred Annex III obligations from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027. 2 August 2028 is the new Annex I date. 2 December 2026 is the Art. 50(2) legacy deadline and the date the new prohibitions apply.

questions.stem: Put these AI Act milestones, as amended by the Digital Omnibus, in chronological order.
options: Digital Omnibus on AI enters into force
Legacy generative systems must meet Article 50(2) marking
Annex III high-risk obligations apply
Annex I product-embedded high-risk obligations apply
questions.explain: The omnibus entered into force on 27 July 2026. Legacy Art. 50(2) marking is due 2 December 2026, Annex III high-risk duties apply from 2 December 2027, and Annex I duties from 2 August 2028.

questions.stem: For each statement about the Digital Omnibus on AI, select Yes if true.

statements.s: It deferred the Article 5 prohibitions that applied from 2 February 2025.
It moved the Annex I product-embedded high-risk deadline from 2 August 2027 to 2 August 2028.
It was adopted as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 and entered into force in July 2026.

questions.explain: The original prohibitions kept their February 2025 date; the omnibus added new bans instead. Annex I moved one year to 2 August 2028. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 was published on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026.

questions.stem: Which new prohibited practice did the Digital Omnibus on AI add to Article 5?
options: AI systems generating non-consensual intimate imagery or child sexual abuse material
All emotion recognition in public spaces
Any use of general-purpose AI models above 10^26 FLOPs
AI-based credit scoring of consumers
questions.explain: The omnibus banned AI systems that generate non-consensual intimate imagery (nudifier apps) and CSAM, applying from 2 December 2026. Emotion recognition outside work and school stays high-risk, large GPAI models are regulated rather than banned, and credit scoring remains Annex III high-risk.

questions.case: A compliance officer argues that because the Digital Omnibus 'softened' Article 4, the company can drop its AI literacy programme entirely.
questions.stem: Which response is most accurate?
options: Correct: the omnibus repealed Article 4
Incorrect: Article 4 now requires certified literacy exams for all staff
Incorrect: the duty remains, reframed as taking measures to promote literacy (an obligation of means)
Correct: AI literacy now applies only to providers of high-risk systems
questions.explain: The omnibus kept Art. 4 but reframed it so providers and deployers must take measures to promote staff AI literacy suited to context, without guaranteeing a set level. It was not repealed, does not require certification, and still covers all providers and deployers.

questions.stem: What is the maximum administrative fine for engaging in a prohibited AI practice under Article 99?
options: EUR 20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover
EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher
EUR 15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover
EUR 7.5 million or 1% of worldwide annual turnover
questions.explain: Prohibited practices carry the top tier: EUR 35 million or 7%, whichever is higher. EUR 20m or 4% is the GDPR maximum. EUR 15m or 3% covers most other obligations, and EUR 7.5m or 1% covers supplying misleading information.

questions.stem: A start-up that qualifies as an SME supplies misleading information to a national competent authority. How is the fine cap calculated?
options: The higher of EUR 7.5 million or 1% of turnover
The higher of EUR 15 million or 3% of turnover
The lower of EUR 15 million or 3% of turnover
The lower of EUR 7.5 million or 1% of turnover
questions.explain: Misleading information falls in the EUR 7.5m or 1% tier. For SMEs and start-ups, Art. 99 caps each fine at the lower of the two amounts, whereas larger undertakings face whichever is higher.

questions.case: A large company with EUR 1 billion worldwide annual turnover breaches its deployer obligations for a high-risk system. Separately, it failed to disclose a deepfake under Article 50.
questions.stem: Which statements about the maximum fines are correct? Select TWO.
options: The deployer breach is capped at EUR 30 million
The Article 50 breach falls in the EUR 35 million or 7% tier
The Article 50 breach falls in the same EUR 15 million or 3% tier as the deployer breach
The deployer breach is capped at EUR 15 million because that figure is fixed
Both breaches are capped at EUR 7.5 million
questions.explain: Deployer and Art. 50 transparency breaches are in the EUR 15m or 3% tier, whichever is higher. For EUR 1bn turnover, 3% is EUR 30m, which exceeds EUR 15m. The 7% tier is for prohibited practices only, and EUR 7.5m is for misleading information.

questions.case: A Canadian company with no EU establishment runs a credit-scoring AI on servers in Canada. It sends scores to a bank in Spain, which uses them to decide on loans to Spanish customers.
questions.stem: Does the AI Act apply to the Canadian company?
options: No, because it has no establishment in the EU
No, because the system runs on servers outside the EU
Only if the bank signs a code of conduct
Yes, because the system's output is used in the Union
questions.explain: Art. 2 covers providers and deployers in third countries where the AI output is used in the Union, and providers placing systems on the EU market wherever they are established. Server location and lack of an EU office do not remove the company from scope.

questions.stem: Which use of AI is excluded from the scope of the AI Act?
options: AI developed and used exclusively for military or defence purposes
A non-EU provider's chatbot offered to EU consumers
An EU bank deploying AI for credit scoring
An importer distributing a US-made high-risk system in Germany
questions.explain: Art. 2 excludes AI used exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes. Non-EU providers serving the EU, EU deployers and importers are all within scope.

questions.stem: On what date did New Zealand's Privacy Act 2020 come into force, replacing the Privacy Act 1993?
options: 1 December 2020
1 July 2020
questions.explain: The Privacy Act 2020 commenced on 1 December 2020. 25 May 2018 is the GDPR date, 1 July 2020 is a plausible but wrong date, and 1 May 2026 is when IPP3A (from the Privacy Amendment Act 2025) took effect.

questions.stem: A Singapore-based e-commerce company has no office or staff in New Zealand but runs a website targeting NZ shoppers and collects their personal information. How does the Privacy Act 2020 apply?
options: It doesn't apply because the company has no place of business in New Zealand
It applies only once the company earns revenue from New Zealand customers
It applies to actions taken in the course of carrying on business in New Zealand
It applies only if the information is stored on servers located in New Zealand
questions.explain: Section 4 applies the Act to overseas agencies for actions in the course of carrying on business in NZ, which doesn't require a place of business, commercial purpose or payment. Server location is irrelevant to this test.

questions.stem: A council wants to add date of birth and gender fields to a dog-registration form, although neither is needed to register a dog. Which principle is most directly engaged?
options: IPP5 storage and security
IPP1 purpose of collection
IPP8 accuracy
IPP13 unique identifiers
questions.explain: IPP1 allows collection only when necessary for a lawful purpose connected with the agency's functions, so unnecessary fields shouldn't be collected. IPP5 concerns security, IPP8 accuracy before use, and IPP13 identifiers.

questions.stem: When collecting personal information directly from an individual, which matters must an agency take reasonable steps to make them aware of under IPP3? Select THREE.
options: The purpose for which the information is being collected
The intended recipients of the information
The agency's annual privacy budget
The individual's rights of access to and correction of the information
The names of the staff members who will view the information
questions.explain: IPP3 requires notice of the fact and purpose of collection, intended recipients, agency name and address, relevant law, whether supply is voluntary, and access/correction rights. Budgets and individual staff names aren't required.

questions.stem: Which change did the Privacy Amendment Act 2025 make to the Information Privacy Principles from 1 May 2026?
options: It added IPP3A, requiring notice when personal information is collected indirectly
It added a GDPR-style right to erasure as IPP14
It replaced IPP12 with an adequacy-decision regime
It made all IPPs enforceable in court against private agencies
questions.explain: The Privacy Amendment Act 2025 inserted IPP3A (notification for indirect collection), in force 1 May 2026. It didn't add an erasure principle, replace IPP12, or change s 31 enforceability.

questions.stem: In June 2026 a debt collection agency buys a portfolio of overdue accounts from a retailer, including debtor contact details. Under IPP3A, who is responsible for notifying the debtors?
options: The retailer, because it originally collected the information
Nobody, because the information was originally collected directly
The Privacy Commissioner, on the agencies' behalf
The debt collection agency, as the indirect collector
questions.explain: IPP3A places the duty on the agency that collects information from someone other than the individual, here the debt collector, unless an exception (such as already aware) applies. The source agency's earlier IPP3 notice doesn't automatically satisfy it.

questions.stem: For each statement about IPP3A exceptions, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Information on a private, access-controlled social media profile counts as publicly available for IPP3A.
An agency investigating suspected fraud may rely on the exception that notice would prejudice the purpose of collection.
The fact that notifying would be inconvenient or require system changes is, on its own, enough to make notice not reasonably practicable.

questions.explain: OPC guidance says access-controlled content isn't publicly available, and inconvenience or incompatible systems alone don't make notice impracticable. Prejudicing the purpose of collection, such as a fraud investigation, is a recognised exception.

questions.stem: A youth sports club plans to collect home addresses from 11-year-old members through an online form with dense legal wording and no parental involvement. Which principle most directly requires the club to reconsider its approach?
options: IPP4 manner of collection
IPP9 retention
IPP11 limits on disclosure
IPP2 source of information
questions.explain: IPP4 requires collection to be lawful, fair and not unreasonably intrusive, taking particular care with children and young people. Retention, disclosure and source principles don't address how fairly the information is gathered from a child.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes IPP5?
options: Agencies must guarantee personal information will never be accessed without authorisation
Agencies must store personal information only on servers in New Zealand
Agencies must protect personal information with security safeguards reasonable in the circumstances
Agencies must encrypt all personal information using approved government algorithms
questions.explain: IPP5 requires reasonable security safeguards against loss and unauthorised access, use, modification or disclosure. It isn't an absolute guarantee, it doesn't impose data localisation, and it doesn't mandate specific encryption algorithms.

questions.stem: An individual requests access to their personal information held by a company. Within what maximum period must the company decide on the request, unless an extension applies?
options: 10 working days
20 working days
30 calendar days
72 hours
questions.explain: The Act requires a decision as soon as reasonably practicable and no later than 20 working days. 30 calendar days is a GDPR-style period, and 72 hours is OPC's breach-notification expectation.

questions.stem: A customer asks an insurer to change a note in their file describing them as 'uncooperative'. The insurer believes the note is accurate and declines. What must the insurer do under IPP7 if the customer asks?
options: Delete the note anyway, because the customer has a right to erasure
Refer the request to the Human Rights Review Tribunal for decision
Take no further action, because the decision is final
Attach the customer's statement of the correction sought to the record
questions.explain: Under IPP7, if an agency declines to correct, it must, on request, take reasonable steps to attach a statement of the correction sought but not made. NZ has no general erasure right, and the HRRT isn't the first decision-maker.

questions.stem: For each statement about retention under IPP9, select Yes if true.
questions.explain: IPP9 sets no fixed period: keep information no longer than required for lawful purposes. Other laws (tax, health) can set minimums, but secure storage doesn't justify keeping data with no remaining purpose.

statements.s: IPP9 requires every agency to keep personal information for exactly seven years.
Another law may require an agency to keep certain information for a minimum period.
Storing information securely justifies keeping it after no lawful purpose remains.

questions.case: Kiwi Fitness collected members' contact and attendance details to manage memberships. Marketing now proposes three new uses: emailing members about a change to class times, sharing attendance data with a supplement brand for its own advertising, and producing aggregated, non-identifying usage statistics for the board.
questions.stem: Which proposed uses can likely proceed under IPP10/IPP11 without new member authorisation? Select TWO.
options: Emailing members about changed class times
Sharing attendance data with the supplement brand
Producing aggregated, non-identifying statistics for the board
Selling member contact lists to a gym equipment retailer
questions.explain: Class-time emails are directly related to managing memberships, and non-identifying statistics fit an IPP10 exception. Giving data to a supplement brand or retailer for their own marketing is an unrelated disclosure needing authorisation under IPP11.

questions.stem: A loyalty programme proposes using customers' IRD (tax) numbers as membership numbers to avoid generating new IDs. Which principle does this most clearly conflict with?
options: IPP12 cross-border disclosure
IPP3 notice of collection
IPP6 access
IPP13 unique identifiers
questions.explain: IPP13 restricts an agency from assigning an identifier it knows another agency has already assigned to the person, and from requiring people to disclose identifiers for unrelated purposes. The other principles don't govern identifier reuse.

questions.stem: For each statement about enforcing the Information Privacy Principles, select Yes if true.

statements.s: An individual's IPP6(1) access entitlement to information held by a public sector agency is enforceable in a court of law.
A customer can sue a private retailer directly in the District Court for breaching IPP5.
The Human Rights Review Tribunal can award damages for an interference with privacy.

questions.explain: Section 31 makes IPPs generally unenforceable in court, except IPP6(1) access against public sector agencies. Other breaches go through the Commissioner and potentially the HRRT, which can award damages.

questions.stem: Under IPP12(1)(a), what must happen before an individual's authorisation can justify disclosure to a foreign recipient?
options: The individual must be expressly informed the recipient may not protect the information with comparable safeguards
The Privacy Commissioner must approve the disclosure in writing
The recipient's country must be prescribed by regulation
The individual must sign a statutory declaration before a lawyer
questions.explain: Authorisation under IPP12(1)(a) is valid only after the agency expressly informs the person that the recipient may not be required to provide comparable protection. No Commissioner approval, prescription or statutory declaration is required for this ground.

questions.stem: Which are grounds under IPP12(1) on which an agency may disclose personal information to a foreign person or entity? Select THREE.
options: The agency reasonably believes the recipient is subject to privacy laws with comparable safeguards
The recipient is carrying on business in New Zealand and the agency reasonably believes it's subject to the Act
The recipient has an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate
The agency reasonably believes the recipient is required by agreement to protect the information comparably
The disclosure is to a company listed on a recognised stock exchange
questions.explain: IPP12(1) grounds include comparable laws, the recipient carrying on business in NZ, and contractual comparable safeguards. Security certification or a stock listing isn't a listed ground, though certification might inform a risk assessment.

questions.case: A NZ fintech wants to rely on IPP12 ground (e), disclosure to a recipient subject to the privacy laws of a prescribed country, when sending data to a partner in the United Kingdom. Its compliance lead checks the current regulations and OPC guidance.
questions.stem: What is the most accurate advice?
options: The UK is prescribed because it has an EU adequacy decision, so ground (e) applies
No countries have been prescribed, so the fintech should rely on another ground such as comparable laws or a contract
Ground (e) applies automatically to any Commonwealth country
The fintech must apply to the Commissioner to have the UK prescribed before disclosing
questions.explain: OPC guidance notes no countries or binding schemes have been prescribed under the regulation-making powers, so ground (e) isn't available. The fintech can use ground (c) after due diligence or ground (f) with model clauses. Adequacy and Commonwealth status don't confer prescription.

questions.stem: A NZ law firm moves its document management system to a cloud provider hosting data in Australia. The provider processes the data only on the firm's instructions and can't use it for its own purposes. How is this treated?
options: It's a disclosure requiring express client authorisation under IPP12(1)(a)
It's a disclosure permitted only because Australia is a prescribed country
It isn't a disclosure, and the firm remains responsible for the information
It isn't a disclosure, and responsibility for the information transfers to the provider
questions.explain: Under s 11, information held by an agent solely on another agency's behalf is treated as held by the principal, so it isn't a disclosure and IPP12 isn't triggered. The firm keeps responsibility for security, access and breach notification.

questions.stem: A SaaS analytics vendor based overseas hosts a NZ retailer's customer data. The vendor's updated terms allow it to use the data to build its own cross-client benchmarking product. What is the main privacy consequence for the retailer?
options: None, because cloud hosting is never a disclosure
The retailer can rely on s 11 provided the data remains encrypted at rest
The vendor must notify the Commissioner instead of the retailer
The vendor is no longer acting only as an agent, so IPP11 and IPP12 must be satisfied
questions.explain: The s 11 agent treatment applies only where the provider doesn't use or disclose the information for its own purposes. Once it does, the transfer becomes a disclosure needing an IPP11 exception and an IPP12 ground. Encryption doesn't change that.

questions.stem: For each statement about the OPC's model contract clauses, select Yes if true.
questions.explain: OPC's model clauses support IPP12(1)(f) and can be adapted to the situation. They're voluntary, and prescribed countries can only be specified by regulation, not by contract.

statements.s: They are designed to help an agency show the overseas recipient must provide comparable safeguards under IPP12.
Agencies must use them unchanged for every overseas disclosure.
Signing them makes the recipient's country a prescribed country.

questions.stem: Personal information about EU residents arrives in New Zealand and is about to be sent on to a third country with no comparable privacy law. Which tool lets the Privacy Commissioner stop the onward transfer?
options: A compliance notice under the IPP12 grounds
A transfer prohibition notice under s 193
An access direction
A code of practice exemption
questions.explain: Section 193 lets the Commissioner prohibit transfers of information received from another country where it's likely to go to a third country without comparable safeguards and would breach OECD basic principles. Access directions and codes don't do this.

questions.stem: For each event, select Yes if it meets the Privacy Act definition of a privacy breach.

statements.s: Ransomware encrypts a client database so the agency can't access it, with no evidence the data was copied.
An employee browses a celebrity customer's records out of curiosity with no work reason.
An agency publishes its own aggregated, non-identifying annual statistics on its website.

questions.explain: A privacy breach includes unauthorised access and actions that prevent the agency accessing information temporarily or permanently. Publishing non-identifying aggregate statistics involves no personal information, so it isn't a privacy breach.

questions.stem: Which statement about privacy breaches under the Privacy Act 2020 is correct?
options: Every privacy breach must be notified to the Commissioner within 72 hours
A privacy breach must be notified only when it has caused or is likely to cause serious harm
Only breaches caused by external attackers count as privacy breaches
Accidental breaches are excluded from the definition
questions.explain: Only notifiable privacy breaches, those that have caused or are likely to cause serious harm, must be notified. The definition covers accidental and internal breaches, not just external attacks.

questions.stem: Which factors are relevant when an agency assesses whether a privacy breach is likely to cause serious harm? Select THREE.
options: Whether the information is protected by a security measure such as encryption
The sensitivity of the personal information involved
The agency's current share price
The person or body that has obtained, or may obtain, the information
Whether the breach happened outside business hours
questions.explain: The Act and OPC list mitigation, sensitivity, the nature of the harm, who has or may obtain the information, and security protections like encryption. Share price and time of day aren't harm factors.

questions.case: A community law centre emails a client update to the wrong recipient. It concerns one client, a family-violence survivor, and includes her new address. The recipient is unknown and hasn't replied to requests to delete the email.
questions.stem: How should the centre treat this breach?
options: Not notifiable, because only one person is affected
Not notifiable, because it was accidental rather than malicious
Notifiable only if the recipient confirms they read the email
Likely notifiable, because sensitive information and a vulnerable person make serious harm likely
questions.explain: Serious harm turns on sensitivity, vulnerability, who may hold the information and mitigation, not record counts or intent. An uncontained address of a family-violence survivor creates a real risk of physical harm, so it's likely notifiable.

questions.stem: According to Office of the Privacy Commissioner guidance, what is the expected timeframe for notifying the Commissioner after an agency becomes aware of a notifiable privacy breach?
options: Within 30 days
Within 20 working days
Ideally within 72 hours
Within 24 hours in all cases
questions.explain: The Act requires notification as soon as practicable, and OPC guidance expects this ideally within 72 hours of becoming aware, even if investigating. 20 working days is the access-request timeframe, and the others aren't NZ requirements.

questions.stem: An agency confirms a breach is likely to cause serious harm but hasn't yet determined the root cause or full number of affected people. What should it do?
options: Notify the Commissioner now with what it knows and update as the investigation progresses
Wait until the investigation is complete so the notification is accurate
Notify only affected individuals, then tell the Commissioner when the investigation ends
Notify the Commissioner only if media coverage is likely
questions.explain: Notification is due as soon as practicable after becoming aware, and OPC accepts incremental notification. Waiting for a complete investigation, skipping the Commissioner, or deciding by media exposure all fail the obligation.

questions.stem: In which circumstance does the Privacy Act permit an agency to delay notifying affected individuals of a notifiable breach?
options: Notifying would cause the agency reputational harm before its annual results
Notifying may create risks for the security of personal information that outweigh the benefits of informing people
The agency hasn't yet notified its cyber insurer
The breach affects fewer than 100 people
questions.explain: Section 116 allows delay only where notification may create risks for the security of personal information that outweigh the benefits, and only while that remains so. Reputation, insurance and small numbers aren't grounds, and Commissioner notification can't be delayed.

questions.case: A retailer's old loyalty database is breached. It contains names and purchase histories of about 40,000 people, but most email and postal addresses are years out of date. Some affected people are under 16.
questions.stem: Which statements correctly describe the retailer's notification options? Select TWO.
options: It may give public notice if notifying people directly isn't reasonably practicable
Outdated contact details mean it need not notify the Commissioner
For a person under 16, if notice would be contrary to their interests, it should consider notifying a representative such as a parent
It may skip individual notification entirely because the data is old
questions.explain: Public notice is used when direct notification isn't reasonably practicable, and s 116 lets agencies notify a representative where notifying an under-16 would be contrary to their interests. Commissioner notification is still required, and data age isn't an exception.

questions.stem: What is the maximum fine for an agency that, without reasonable excuse, fails to notify the Privacy Commissioner of a notifiable privacy breach?
options: 4% of global annual turnover
questions.explain: Failing to notify the Commissioner without reasonable excuse is an offence with a maximum fine of NZD 10,000. Turnover-based penalties belong to the GDPR, and the higher dollar figures aren't in the Privacy Act 2020.

questions.stem: What is NotifyUs?
options: The National Cyber Security Centre's incident ticketing portal
The Office of the Privacy Commissioner's online tool for assessing and reporting privacy breaches
A Police service for reporting identity theft
A mandatory customer notification email template set by regulation
questions.explain: NotifyUs is OPC's online breach notification tool, including a self-assessment for serious harm. The NCSC and Police have their own reporting channels, and no regulation prescribes a customer email template.

questions.stem: A staff member emails a client spreadsheet to the wrong external address. Put the OPC breach response steps in order.
options: Contain: recall the email and ask the recipient to delete it
Assess: evaluate sensitivity, who received it and the likelihood of serious harm
Notify: report via NotifyUs and tell affected clients if serious harm is likely
Prevent: review the root cause and add controls such as external-recipient warnings
questions.explain: OPC's breach guidance is contain, assess, notify, prevent. Containment limits damage first, assessment decides notifiability, notification follows promptly, and prevention addresses the root cause.

questions.stem: What kind of body is New Zealand's Privacy Commissioner?
options: A government department reporting to the Minister of Justice
A division of the Ombudsman's office
A court of record
An independent Crown entity
questions.explain: The Privacy Commissioner is an independent Crown entity, Crown-funded but independent in its statutory functions. It isn't a department, part of the Ombudsman or a court; the Human Rights Review Tribunal is the adjudicating body.

questions.stem: A patient believes a private clinic disclosed her information without authority and the matter can't be resolved directly. Put the typical escalation path in order.
options: Raise the concern with the clinic's privacy officer
Complain to the Privacy Commissioner, who investigates and tries to settle
The Commissioner refers the unresolved complaint to the Director of Human Rights Proceedings
The Director brings proceedings in the Human Rights Review Tribunal
questions.explain: Complainants usually start with the agency, then the Commissioner investigates and conciliates. Unresolved justified complaints can be referred to the Director of Human Rights Proceedings, who may bring proceedings in the HRRT.

questions.stem: OPC finds an agency keeps sending client information to wrong recipients because of poor processes, although no one has complained. Which power can require the agency to fix its processes?
options: An access direction
A compliance notice
A transfer prohibition notice
A code of practice exemption
questions.explain: A compliance notice requires an agency to do or stop doing something to comply with the Act and doesn't depend on a complaint. Access directions are limited to IPP6 complaints, and transfer prohibition notices cover onward transfers.

questions.stem: For each statement about the Commissioner's binding powers, select Yes if true.

statements.s: An access direction can be issued after investigating an IPP6 access complaint.
An agency can appeal a compliance notice to the Human Rights Review Tribunal.
The Commissioner can issue an access direction requiring an agency to delete inaccurate information under IPP7.

questions.explain: Access directions follow IPP6 complaints and can be appealed to the HRRT, as can compliance notices. Access directions don't cover IPP7 correction; correction issues go through the usual complaint process or a compliance notice.

questions.stem: For each statement about Privacy Act codes of practice, select Yes if true.
questions.explain: Codes are binding secondary legislation that can modify, exempt from or prescribe how IPPs apply to a sector, activity or information type. Breaching a code rule is treated as breaching an IPP.

statements.s: A code can modify how the IPPs apply to a particular industry or type of information.
A breach of a code rule is treated like a breach of an IPP for complaints.
Codes are voluntary guidance with no legal effect.

questions.stem: A supermarket chain plans to use facial recognition to identify people on a watchlist entering its stores. Which code of practice specifically governs this activity?
options: Telecommunications Information Privacy Code 2020
Credit Reporting Privacy Code 2020
Justice Sector Unique Identifier Code 2020
Biometric Processing Privacy Code 2025
questions.explain: The Biometric Processing Privacy Code 2025 covers agencies using biometric processing such as facial recognition, in force from 3 November 2025. The telecommunications, credit and justice codes cover other sectors and identifiers.

questions.stem: Which are codes of practice issued under the Privacy Act 2020? Select THREE.
options: Health Information Privacy Code 2020
Telecommunications Information Privacy Code 2020
Credit Reporting Privacy Code 2020
Anti-Money Laundering Privacy Code 2021
Consumer Data Right Privacy Code 2025
questions.explain: The HIPC, Telecommunications and Credit Reporting codes are current Privacy Act codes, alongside the Biometric Processing code and others. There is no Anti-Money Laundering or Consumer Data Right privacy code issued by the Commissioner.

questions.stem: Which body can award damages for humiliation, loss of dignity and injury to feelings caused by an interference with privacy?
options: The Human Rights Review Tribunal
The Privacy Commissioner
The Ombudsman
The Director of Human Rights Proceedings
questions.explain: The HRRT can award damages, including for humiliation, loss of dignity and injury to feelings. The Commissioner investigates and settles, the Director brings proceedings, and the Ombudsman handles official information complaints.

questions.stem: Which actions are offences under the Privacy Act 2020? Select TWO.
options: Pretending to be an individual to mislead an agency into releasing that individual's information
Charging a reasonable fee for a private sector access request
Destroying personal information knowing an access request for it has been made
Taking 18 working days to respond to an access request
questions.explain: Impersonating someone to obtain their information and destroying requested information are offences with fines up to $10,000. Private agencies may charge reasonably in some cases, and 18 working days is within the 20-working-day limit.

questions.stem: A four-person landscaping business asks whether it must have a privacy officer. What is the correct answer?
options: No, only agencies with more than 50 employees must appoint one
Yes, every agency must appoint at least one privacy officer, who may be inside or outside the agency
Yes, but the privacy officer must hold a practising certificate as a lawyer
No, small businesses can rely on the Privacy Commissioner to act as their privacy officer
questions.explain: Section 201 requires every agency (except individuals acting for personal or domestic affairs) to appoint one or more privacy officers, internal or external. There is no size threshold or legal qualification requirement.

questions.stem: How does the Health Information Privacy Code 2020 relate to the Information Privacy Principles?
options: Its rules apply in addition to the IPPs, so health agencies must satisfy both
It is non-binding guidance on how health agencies might apply the IPPs
Its rules replace the IPPs for health information held by health agencies
It only applies to public hospitals
questions.explain: The HIPC is a code of practice whose rules take the place of the IPPs for health information held by health agencies. It is binding, and it covers private as well as public health agencies, from GPs to insurers.

questions.stem: For each statement about the HIPC's scope, select Yes if true.

statements.s: A private pharmacy is a health agency under the HIPC.
A GP practice's payroll records for its own staff are health information under the HIPC.
ACC is among the agencies the HIPC applies to.

questions.explain: Pharmacies are health service providers and ACC is a listed agency, so the HIPC applies. Staff payroll records aren't health information about patients, so the IPPs apply to them.

questions.stem: In July 2026 a hospital receives a referral from a GP containing a patient's history. Which HIPC rule requires the hospital to take reasonable steps to make the patient aware it has collected this information?
options: Rule 3A
Rule 3
Rule 8
Rule 11
questions.explain: Rule 3A, in force 1 May 2026, applies when a health agency collects health information from someone other than the individual or their representative. Rule 3 covers direct collection, rule 8 accuracy, and rule 11 disclosure.

questions.case: A genetic counsellor collects details from a patient about her parents' and siblings' medical conditions to build a family history. The relatives haven't been contacted. The clinic asks whether rule 3A means it must notify each relative.
questions.stem: What is the best advice?
options: Yes, every relative must be notified as soon as reasonably practicable
Yes, but only relatives aged over 16
No, the code exempts information collected from the individual to assemble a family or genetic history
No, rule 3A applies only to public sector health agencies
questions.explain: HIPC rule 3A includes a health-specific exception for information collected from the individual to assemble their family or genetic history. Rule 3A isn't limited to public sector agencies and has no age-based relative test.

questions.stem: Which HIPC rule requires health information to be collected directly from the individual concerned, unless an exception applies?
options: Rule 1
Rule 4
Rule 5
Rule 2
questions.explain: Rule 2 is the source rule: collect from the individual unless an exception applies. Rule 1 covers purpose, rule 4 manner of collection, and rule 5 storage and security.

questions.stem: A patient makes her first request to a private dermatology clinic for a copy of her clinical notes. The clinic proposes a $45 administration fee. What does the HIPC say?
options: The fee is fine, since private agencies may always charge a reasonable fee
The fee is allowed only if the clinic gives an estimate first
The clinic must refer the request to the Ministry of Health
Private health agencies generally can't charge for access, apart from narrow exceptions such as repeat requests or certain images
questions.explain: The HIPC's charging clause stops private health agencies charging for access except in limited cases, such as a repeat request within 12 months or copies of x-rays, videos or MRI/PET/CAT scans. A general admin fee on a first request isn't permitted.

questions.stem: A new GP clinic is setting up its approach to HIPC rule 5. Put OPC's suggested security planning steps in order.
options: Identify the risks to the health information it holds
Make a security plan covering electronic, operational and physical security
Put the plan into practice
Review and update security on an ongoing basis as risks change
questions.explain: OPC's rule 5 guidance: identify risks, plan safeguards across electronic, operational and physical security, implement the plan, and treat security as ongoing, raising the standard as risks or sensitivity grow.

questions.stem: A GP believes a patient with an uncontrolled seizure condition is continuing to drive a school bus, despite advice, creating a serious risk to children. Which HIPC basis most directly supports disclosure to the relevant authority?
options: Rule 11 exception to prevent or lessen a serious threat to public safety
Rule 10 directly related purpose
Rule 12 cross-border disclosure ground
Rule 3A indirect collection exception
questions.explain: Rule 11 permits disclosure where necessary to prevent or lessen a serious threat to public health or safety, to someone who can act on it. Rule 10 governs use, rule 12 overseas disclosure, and rule 3A notice for indirect collection.

questions.stem: According to OPC guidance on HIPC rule 9, how long must health care providers generally keep patient health information under Health Act regulations?
options: At least 10 years from the last encounter with the patient
Seven years from the date of collection
Until the patient turns 25
No minimum; destroy as soon as treatment ends
questions.explain: OPC notes Health Act regulations require providers to keep health information for 10 years from the last encounter, unless it's transferred to another provider or the patient. Rule 9 otherwise limits retention to what is required.

questions.stem: A private school wants to record students' National Health Index (NHI) numbers as their primary enrolment ID. Under HIPC rule 13, why is this a problem?
options: The NHI may only be stored in New Zealand-hosted systems
Rule 13 limits NHI assignment to authorised or listed health agencies, and requiring it for an unrelated purpose is restricted
NHI numbers expire when a child turns 16
The school would need written approval from the Privacy Commissioner
questions.explain: Only agencies authorised by law or listed in the HIPC schedule may assign the NHI, and people shouldn't be required to disclose a unique identifier for unrelated purposes. There's no data-residency rule, expiry or Commissioner approval mechanism.

questions.case: A private radiology provider discovers that an attacker accessed its patient portal and downloaded scan reports for 2,300 patients. Some patients have serious diagnoses not yet discussed with them by their specialists.
questions.stem: Which response best reflects the Privacy Act and HIPC?
options: Follow only the HIPC, because the Privacy Act breach rules don't apply to health agencies
Notify affected patients but not the Commissioner, as health information is covered by the HIPC
Notify the Commissioner promptly, and assess the health-prejudice exception for specific patients with their practitioners
Delay all notifications until every specialist has discussed results with their patients
questions.explain: Part 6 of the Privacy Act applies to health agencies. The Commissioner must be notified as soon as practicable; for individuals where notice would likely prejudice their health, s 116 allows not notifying them after consulting their practitioner, considering representatives. Blanket delay isn't permitted.
